title: Business-class fare on a domestic route (Vistara)

source.note: The book names Vistara, Air India and Jet. Reset here as an unnamed premium airline because Jet stopped flying in 2019 and Vistara merged into Air India in November 2024.

prompt: How should a premium full-service airline price its business-class ticket on a domestic route? Start wherever you think is appropriate.

facts.asks: When the candidate first asks about the customer segment
facts.reveal: Why do you need to know that?
A premium full-service airline: newer aircraft, more consistent business-class cabins, and higher service quality than most competitors on this route.
It depends on the flight timing: one full-service rival on some slots, another on others. Does that matter?

facts.asks: When the candidate lists cost, value and competition as approaches
After the candidate gives fares by time of day
facts.reveal: Is the time of day the only factor you would consider to determine demand?

acceptedAssumptions: Business class gives 2–3 productive hours, worth ₹3,000–5,000 to someone earning ₹20–30 lakh a year
outOfScope: Anything about real airlines beyond the facts given

crux.statement: Cost cannot guide the price. Triangulate value and competition, and vary the fare by time slot and season, because competitive intensity depends on who flies that slot.
crux.clue: "It depends on the flight timing." That signals slot-based pricing.

paths: Rule out cost → value to a business traveller → competitive band → fare by slot and season

quant.working: Rough check on the candidate's own inputs: ₹25 lakh a year over about 2,000 working hours ≈ ₹1,250 an hour; × 2.5 hours ≈ ₹3,100, the low end of the ₹3,000–5,000 range. Added to the ₹10,000 economy fare this supports about ₹13,000–15,000 on time value alone, so the competitive band, not time value, sets the fare.
quant.answer: Time value is roughly ₹3,100 a flight, or about ₹13,000–15,000 with the economy fare

answerKey: A range, not one number, set inside the competitive band with a modest premium
Higher fares on morning and evening peak slots than at mid-day, with the reason
A seasonal lift at festivals, long weekends and year-end

close.condition: The candidate has ruled out cost and proposed a fare or range.
close.prompt: So what fares would you set, and how would they vary?

anchors.s7: Rules out cost, uses value and competition, gives a range.
anchors.s9: Prices by slot and season, explains why, and checks the value logic against the economy fare.

verifierFlags.decision: Reset as an unnamed premium full-service airline with two unnamed full-service rivals. The book's names stay in the source note only.

verifierFlags.text: The book's ₹30,000 "value ceiling" does not follow from the inputs given.
verifierFlags.decision: Dropped from the expected logic. No answer is graded against ₹30,000, and the book's ₹22,000–28,000 fares are not treated as the right answer.

verifierFlags.text: Competitor fares of ₹20,000–25,000 are the candidate's assumption, listed as a fact on the summary page.
verifierFlags.decision: Kept as an accepted assumption. The interviewer does not supply competitor fares.

verifierFlags.text: The book's last probe asks whether "day of the week" is the only factor, though the candidate had priced by time of day.
verifierFlags.decision: Reworded to "time of day" so the probe follows from the candidate's answer.
